S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
examples: Desk, bag, or room is always messy and remains disorganized.
Unable to prioritize or determine the order of tasks, starting them randomly.
Fails to plan time effectively, frequently missing deadlines or rushing to finish at the last minute.
Feels overwhelmed by how to start multi-step projects and procrastinates.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
examples: Continually procrastinates or is reluctant to start writing long reports or complex homework.
Avoids activities that require long periods of concentration, such as reading books or studying.
Passes off tasks that require complex thinking or planning to others.
Gets annoyed or resists when asked to start a task that requires significant mental effort.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
examples: Frequently loses school supplies or office supplies like pens, erasers, and calculators.
Always searching for glasses, cell phones, wallets, or keys because they do not know where they are.
Loses necessary documents or materials at home or in the office and cannot find them.
Cannot remember where they placed an item they were holding just moments ago.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
examples: Easily distracted and stops working due to small noises or movements nearby.
Cannot concentrate because eyes keep wandering to the scenery outside the window or people passing by.
Starts daydreaming or gets sidetracked by sudden thoughts while working or studying.
Loses focus and listens in when hearing side conversations or TV sounds.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
examples: Forgets appointment times or meeting schedules, arriving late or missing them entirely.
Forgets to reply to received calls or messages for days.
Frequently incurs late fees because of missing deadlines for utility bills or credit card payments.
Forgets to take medication or leaves necessary items at home when going out.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
examples: Frequently leaves seat or wanders around during class or meetings using excuses.
Unable to sit still during meals and keeps getting up.
Leaves seat in the middle of a movie or performance to go to the restroom or go outside.
Continually leaves seat and wanders around in the office where one is expected to sit and work.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention that interferes with functioning or development, with relatively fewer or no prominent hyperactive-impulsive symptoms. Individuals often have longstanding difficulties with sustained focus, organization, following through on tasks, and managing details, though these issues may not become clinically significant until environmental demands exceed their compensatory strategies. In adults and older adolescents, the disorder commonly presents as chronic disorganization, mental distractibility, and forgetfulness rather than overt behavioral disruption, and may be misattributed to stress, personality traits, or normal aging. Diagnosis requires symptom onset in childhood, cross-situational impairment, and careful differentiation from cognitive disorders, mood and anxiety disorders, or effects of medical illness and substances.

patient.stressor: For most of her life, Lissette’s meticulous approach to cooking, gardening, and running church events allowed her to mask long‑standing distractibility and reliance on written lists. About a year and a quarter ago, her husband developed more complex health needs, and she took on coordinating his appointments, medications, and insurance in addition to her usual senior center volunteering. The added caregiving responsibilities, with more phone calls, paperwork, and time‑sensitive details, overwhelmed the informal systems she had relied on for decades, leading to mounting errors in scheduling and missed follow‑through that she initially blamed on "getting old." After a near‑miss where she confused her husband’s medication timing and a friend at church gently pointed out similar patterns in her volunteer work, her primary care physician referred her for a psychiatric evaluation to sort out whether this was early dementia or a longstanding attention problem becoming more visible.
patient.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep forgetting everyday things—calls I promised to make, appointments I just wrote down, even simple errands—and it’s starting to cause problems with my husband’s care.”

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
S005.manifestation: These days when I sit down to sort out my husband’s appointments, my volunteering, and our bills, I just end up with little piles of papers and half‑filled calendars all over the dining table, and I can’t seem to decide what to tackle first so everything gets jumbled and rushed at the last minute.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
S006.manifestation: If I know I have to sit and really concentrate on something—like filling out his insurance forms online or reading through discharge instructions—I’ll keep finding excuses to put it off, because my brain feels tired before I even start and I dread how quickly I’ll lose track of what I’m doing.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
S007.manifestation: I’m constantly misplacing things I need, like setting my glasses or the pill organizer down in the kitchen and then spending ten minutes walking from room to room looking for them, even though I just had them in my hand.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
S008.manifestation: When I’m on the phone scheduling his doctor visits or trying to read a recipe, the smallest thing—a bird at the feeder, the TV my husband has on in the other room, or even my own thought about something I need from the store—pulls my mind away, and I realize I’ve missed what the person just said or lost my place on the page.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
S009.manifestation: Over the past year I keep forgetting everyday things I’ve promised to do—calling the cardiologist back, picking up a prescription on the way home, even simple chores like putting the laundry in the dryer—so I end up apologizing a lot and double‑checking with people because I don’t trust my memory anymore.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
S010.manifestation: I’ve noticed that when I’m sitting through a long church meeting or waiting with my husband at the clinic, I’m always tapping my foot, rubbing my hands together, or shifting around in the chair without really meaning to, like I just can’t get fully comfortable staying still.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
S011.manifestation: During longer events, like Bible study or my husband’s appointments, I find myself getting up to straighten the coffee table, use the restroom, or “check on something,” because sitting in one spot for too long makes me restless and antsy even though I know I’m supposed to stay put.

add_requirements.onset_prior_to_12_years: Even back in grade school, my teachers would write on my report cards that I was a bright girl but always daydreaming, losing track of instructions, and forgetting to turn in homework unless my mother stood over me and checked my backpack.
add_requirements.functional_impairment: Because I keep losing track of appointments and mixing up times or follow-up calls, my husband has almost missed important tests, and I’ve pulled back from volunteering at the senior center and church because I’m afraid I’ll let people down or make a serious mistake.
add_requirements.duration: These problems have really stood out and interfered with my day-to-day life for about the past year and a few months, ever since my husband’s health needs and all the related paperwork and appointments ramped up.
